Q: How to count distinct concurrent resource max usage using a mysql query? A:

Consider solution with steps:

  1. Create datetime grid ("events_grid") - list of all "datetime" values from source. At every event_dtm we have events - start or stop use resource.
  2. JOIN source table to grid on dt_from<=event_dtm and dt_to>event_dtm - so row belongs to this point.
    We use "dt_to>event_dtm" instead of "dt_to>=event_dtm" considering range as [dt_from,dt_to). Other words, dt_from is included to range, dt_to excluded from range.
  3. Count DISTINCT resource_id for event_dtm ("qty"). Also take this count from previous row. If in this point "qty" is changed - we start new group ("grn"), as always in "gaps and islands" tasks.
  4. Group rows and take qty, min(event_dtm) as dt_from, min(event_dtm) from next row as end of range (up to).

See example.

with events_grid as(
  select dt_from event_dtm from test
  union
  select dt_to event_dtm from test
)
,resource_events as(
select * 
from events_grid d
left join test t on t.dt_from<=d.event_dtm and t.dt_to>d.event_dtm
)
,periods_qty as(
select event_dtm,qty,prev_qty
  ,sum(case when qty=prev_qty then 0 else 1 end)over(order by event_dtm) grn
from(
select event_dtm,count(distinct resource_id) qty
  ,lag(count(distinct resource_id))over(order by event_dtm) prev_qty
from resource_events
group by event_dtm
)t
)
select grn,min(event_dtm) dt_from
  ,lead(min(event_dtm))over(order by grn) dt_to
  ,min(qty) qty
from periods_qty
group by grn
order by grn

Q: Can I have a vector that shares storage with another vector? A:

In a word, no. std::vector just doesn't do that. But there are two similar things you can do:

  1. A vector of pointers (perhaps std::shared_ptr), such that one vector points at elements from the other. Of course, now you have a vector of pointers to the object, not the object, which may be a problem. One possible idea is std::reference_wrapper, but it's not great.

  2. There's also std::span, which is made for this use case.

Q: One, Two and Three Column Layouts A:

Move the entire /*Begin Desktop*/ block to the very bottom of your CSS file, after the Tablet block.

CSS is generally best organized from smallest screens to largest. By placing the Desktop code last, it ensures that when a screen is large enough to be a desktop, the desktop rules override the tablet rules.

Also, in your <head> change viewpoint to viewport.

Q: CS50 PSET 4 "Speller" - Having issues freeing allocated memory A:

This took a bit to track down, but the good comments regarding using the -fsanitize flag helped zero in on the issue. First off, I added in the compiler option "-fsanitize=address" along with the linkage to the "asan" library (-lasan).

-fsanitize=address

-lasan

Along with that, I temporarily inserted print statements in various functions, compiled the code, and reviewed the output. After multiple passes, I was able to narrow down the issue to the check function.

// Returns true if word is in dictionary (case insensitive), else false
bool check(const char *word)
{
    // TODO
    int index = hash(word);
    node *cursor = table[index];
    while (cursor != NULL)
    {
        printf("Node value address: %p  word: %s\n", cursor, cursor->word);
        if (strcasecmp(word, cursor->word) == 0)
        {
            return true;
        }
        cursor = cursor->next;
        printf("cursor now is: %p\n", cursor);
    }
    return false;
}

The statement to be evaluated was when the cursor work variable was being updated with the next cursor value. The expectation was that when the end of the list was reached, the next cursor value would be nil, but that wasn't necessarily the case as is seen in the following terminal output.

==6327==ABORTING

As noted, the next cursor value contains some undefined memory address value which is causing the sanitizer to complain and abort the program. Backtracking, this issue is actually due to the initial usage of an array entry in the "table" structure array in the dictionary load function.

    while (fscanf(file, "%s", word_list) != EOF) // reads one word
    {
        node *node_word = malloc(sizeof(node));
        if (node_word == NULL) // checks if there is enough memory for the node
        {
            return false;
        }
        counter++;
        strcpy(node_word->word, word_list); // copies the already read word into the node
        // prepends each new word in a linked list at table[index]
        int index = hash(word_list); // finds which index this word belongs in the hash table
        if (table[index] == NULL) // checks if there are any words in linked-list
        {
            table[index] = node_word; // the root points to newly-"read" word and that word marks beginning of linked list
            /* next pointer can contain uninitialized data  */
        }
        else
        {
            struct node *next = table[index]; // creates a node that points beginning of linked list at that index
            table[index] = node_word; // the root points to our newly-"read" word
            node_word->next = next; // newly-"read" word points to "second" (if there is one) word in linked list
        }
        numWords++; // increments numWords, which is returned in size()
    }
    fclose(file);

When a table array element is first used, its next node pointer value needs to be initialized to NULL to ensure that the subsequent checking process comes to a proper exit in the while loop. With that, following is the refactored code within the "if" test.

    if (table[index] == NULL) // checks if there are any words in linked-list
    {
        table[index] = node_word; // the root points to newly-"read" word and that word marks beginning of linked list
        table[index]->next = NULL; /* Ensure the next pointer is initialized    */
    }

Rerunning the test illustrates that when the end of a list is reached within the check function, the next node pointer is indeed nil.

cursor now is: (nil)

The things to take away here is that if diagnostic programs like the checker program hints at possible memory leaks or memory issues, it is beneficial to utilize tutorials on memory tools such as valgrind and/or utilization of additional compiler directives such as "-fsanitize".

Q: Is it possible to eliminate the this pointer in a singleton? A:

You can also make the debug function static, and inside that function use the static instance.
This way you get rid of the this pointers.

So the question remains, why use an instance?

This is usually used to to hide the static variable and lazily initialize the variable at the moment the function is called for the first time.

Since C++11 this initialization is also thread safe.
